strings.name: Han Kang
strings.role: Novelist and poet · Bodies, violence and historical memory
strings.summary: Writing in Korean, Han Kang approaches historical violence, mourning and human vulnerability through bodily experience and intimate relationships. The Vegetarian depicts resistance to bodily expectations; Human Acts responds to Gwangju, and We Do Not Part examines traumatic memory on Jeju. Her poetic prose retains the specificity of history. She shared the 2016 International Booker Prize with her translator and received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Literature.

strings.influence.rationale: Addressed historical trauma and lived experience in works including The Vegetarian and Human Acts, bringing Korean literature to readers worldwide.

strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: Graduated in Korean language and literature from Yonsei University in 1993
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Bodies in conflict with society
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: The Vegetarian explores desire, violence and bodily autonomy through a family’s disruption; Han shared the International Booker with Deborah Smith.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Witnessing historical trauma
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Human Acts and We Do Not Part connect individual mourning with collective memories of Gwangju and Jeju.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Joins a literature and music event in Berlin
strings.timeline.event-01.text: At the Philharmonie’s chamber hall she discussed music and writing during Satzwechsel, which included readings from Light and Thread.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Publishes Light and Thread
strings.timeline.event-02.text: The essay collection reflects on reading, writing and life; it later featured alongside her fiction at international reading events.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Receives the Nobel Prize in Literature
strings.timeline.event-03.text: The Swedish Academy recognized prose confronting historical trauma and human vulnerability, drawing new international attention to Korean literature.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Publishes We Do Not Part
strings.timeline.event-04.text: Promises, memories and a journey address the Jeju April 3 events, connecting historical violence with continuing grief.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: The Vegetarian wins the International Booker
strings.timeline.event-05.text: She shared the award with English translator Deborah Smith, bringing her Korean-language work to a broader readership.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Publishes Human Acts
strings.timeline.event-06.text: Set around the 1980 Gwangju crackdown, the novel examines violence and its lasting aftermath through victims, survivors and witnesses.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Publishes The Vegetarian
strings.timeline.event-07.text: A woman’s refusal to eat meat unsettles family relationships, exposing tensions between social demands and personal agency.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Publishes her first story collection
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Love of Yeosu gathered early fiction after her poetry debut, establishing a practice across literary forms.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Graduates and publishes poetry
strings.timeline.event-09.text: After graduating from Yonsei, she published poems in Literature and Society, beginning her public literary career.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in Gwangju
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Born in Gwangju and moved to Seoul at nine; a literary family provided a context for her early reading and writing.
